cards.title: View Copywriting as Scalable Persuasion
cards.summary: Reframe writing as one-to-many persuasion that scales infinitely, motivating content and email strategy.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in written content, email, or long-form product descriptions versus one-to-one selling.
steps: Recognize that nearly all ecommerce copy — product pages, emails, ads, blog posts — is persuasion, not self-expression; the goal is to move a reader toward an action.
Aim content at a scalable audience: a single well-crafted piece can convert unlimited readers, unlike a one-to-one sales conversation.
Identify the specific persuasion goal before writing: join list, click buy button, share, or forward to a friend.
Use this framing to justify consistent investment in copy quality, since the same piece keeps working without being rewritten.
caveats: The presenter's $20M figure refers to personal experience selling online via email; specific revenue outcomes are examples, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Begin With the End in Mind: Emotion, Action, Takeaway
cards.summary: Decide the reaction, action, and single takeaway before writing to structure any piece of store copy.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, landing page, welcome email, or campaign piece and unsure what to lead with.
steps: Before typing, pick the specific emotion you want the reader to feel (awe, outrage, heartwarming, curiosity — the source cites a viral-video agency that chose emotion first, then scripted).
Decide the single action you want: click buy, share, subscribe, or forward.
Write down the one sentence or line you want remembered if they forget everything else — people remember sentences, not whole documents.
For Shopify product pages this means naming a shareable hook and the buy action before drafting the description.
Use the takeaway sentence as a substitute for a formal outline, then draft around it.
caveats: Emotion-first scripting is a technique from a viral video context; its translation to product copy is the presenter's assertion, not a tested ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Warm Up With Copywork Before Writing
cards.summary: Hand-copy strong writing to absorb rhythm, structure, and persuasive cadence before drafting your own.
cards.use_when: Facing a high-stakes store page, sales email, or campaign and feeling blocked or stale.
steps: Pick a piece of writing you admire — a blog post, script, or landing page that demonstrates the style you want.
Do not outline; instead copy the text word-for-word by hand (typing is a fallback if handwriting isn't possible).
Resist adding or improving anything — the goal is absorption, not editing.
Spend 10–15 minutes on this warm-up, treating it like a pre-workout warm-up rather than the actual session.
Keep different source pieces for different tones (persuasive, serious business, etc.) and rotate them based on what you're about to write.
caveats: The source describes doing this two hours daily for eight months to learn writing; short sessions are a maintenance version for experienced writers.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Four-Step Writing Process: Copywork, Draft, Incubate, Edit
cards.summary: Sequence store content through warm-up, ugly fast draft, an incubation gap, then editing where the value is created.
cards.use_when: Producing any substantial copy — a launch email, product page, or content piece — where quality matters more than speed.
steps: Warm up with copywork on admired writing for 10–15 minutes.
Draft fast and badly — a brain dump — without self-censorship and without showing anyone.
Incubate: step away from the text, with the source suggesting at least 90 minutes, sometimes six hours or 1–2 days, while doing something passive like walking, cooking, or showering.
Return and edit hard — editing, not drafting, is where the value is created (the source cites 'I'm a lousy writer but a good editor').
Shift your time ratio toward editing rather than trying to produce a perfect draft, which causes fatigue and doubt.
Aim for a short draft followed by a high-energy edit after the incubation gap.
caveats: Incubation durations are the presenters' heuristics, not measured optima; choose a gap that fits your production timeline.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Edit for Readability: Low Grade Level, No Jargon, No Adverbs
cards.summary: Write store copy at a fifth-to-eighth-grade reading level and strip jargon, adverbs, and thesaurus words.
cards.use_when: Finalizing product descriptions, explainer content, or email copy to maximize comprehension and conversion.
steps: Target a fifth-to-eighth-grade reading level and verify with a readability checker such as the Hemingway app.
Eliminate jargon and corporate words you'd never say aloud — the source singles out 'utilize' as a LinkedIn tell.
Avoid adverbs and cut fluff; on the internet shorter is generally better than longer as long as the meaning holds.
Vary sentence length to create a musical rhythm across paragraphs.
Apply Stephen King's rule (cited by the source): any word you have to hunt for in a thesaurus is the wrong word — no exceptions.
Say the sentence aloud; if you wouldn't say it that way, rewrite it as you would say it.
caveats: Low reading levels are a marketing default, not a universal rule — technical or compliance copy may require precise terminology.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Don't Bury the Lead: Punch With the First Sentence
cards.summary: Open with the most provocative, promising, or surprising sentence rather than context or background.
cards.use_when: Writing the opening of a landing page, founder story, or email where a reader decides in seconds whether to continue.
steps: Cut the intro, context, and background — most openers can be trimmed to roughly the last couple of sentences and be stronger.
Move the thesis, the promise, or the provocative statement to the very top.
Use the Soylent-style opener as a model: state the strange thing you did and immediately pose the implicit question ('why would I do something so stupid? I'll explain').
Test by covering everything except the first two sentences: if an indifferent reader wouldn't need to read the next sentence, rewrite it.
Repeat the test sentence by sentence; once the reader has invested through three or four sentences, you can let the piece breathe and add context.
caveats: The source notes that 80–90% of readers only read the headline, meaning a weak headline squanders the rest of the copy — but the exact share is the presenters' estimate, not measured data.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Use Curiosity Gaps Without Faking the Payoff
cards.summary: Grab attention by withholding just enough, and pay off the hook quickly and truthfully.
cards.use_when: Crafting subject lines, ad hooks, or page openers that need to earn the next click or scroll.
steps: Punch the reader's attention with a strong opening, but don't reveal everything — hold back enough to make them continue.
Deliver the payoff soon after the hook, not ten minutes later in the piece.
Distinguish sensational-but-true from clickbait: the source's rule is 'it ain't bait if you deliver on the promise.'
Test the line against the test: would an indifferent reader need to read the next sentence?
To build the capability, maintain a swipe file of headlines and openers that grabbed you emotionally, so you have proven patterns ready.
caveats: False promises damage trust; the source is explicit that if you don't pay off the hook soon, it becomes bad copy.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Test Ideas and Words by Speaking Them First
cards.summary: If you can't explain it plainly out loud, the idea isn't ready — spoken language becomes the copy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing copy from a team member or drafting product explanations and founder messaging.
steps: When someone sends you a long draft, ask them to explain it out loud in plain language instead of reading the document.
When they give the one-sentence version, that sentence becomes the first line; often it's all the copy needs.
Write as you talk — the most engaging writing feels like a direct conversation with the reader.
If you can't even say it clearly, don't write it yet; clarify the underlying thinking first.
Treat informal language as compatible with professional: informal is not the opposite of professional (the source's claim, demonstrated with plain-spoken examples).
caveats: The informal-can-be-professional position is a strong opinion from the presenters; regulated categories or luxury positioning may warrant a more formal register.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Build Swipe Files for Phrases, Openers, and Closers
cards.summary: Accumulate standout phrases and structures in categorized files so strong copy patterns are ready before you write.
cards.use_when: Everyday store content production — product pages, newsletter intros, campaign emails.
steps: Whenever you read or hear something that lands emotionally, capture the exact phrasing immediately in a notes app or file.
Categorize by use case: phrases, headlines, connecting words, openers, and closers (the source keeps separate opener and closer files because those were his hardest sections).
Collect from diverse sources — podcasters, YouTubers, competitors, other brands' site copy.
Before writing a new piece, pull two or three applicable swipe entries and riff on their structure rather than copying them verbatim into customer-facing copy.
Apply swipe files to common ecommerce artifacts: landing pages, product descriptions, and email intros/outros.
caveats: Use swipes as structural inspiration; directly copying competitor copy into your store creates legal and brand risk.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Apply Intention-and-Obstacle Storytelling to Brand Copy
cards.summary: Frame brand and founder stories around a clear intention blocked by obstacles, elevating emotional stakes.
cards.use_when: Writing About-Us pages, brand origin stories, or narrative-driven product pages and campaigns.
steps: Define the central character's intention — what the brand, founder, or customer is trying to achieve.
Name the obstacle standing in the way; the tension between intention and obstacle creates the narrative arc (attributed to Aaron Sorkin's framework).
Elevate stakes even in low-stakes situations so the emotion lands.
Avoid burying the lead in the story — hit with the provocative or curious opening first, then build context once the reader is invested.
Let the founder's authentic voice show through; transparent communication reads as more credible to buyers.
caveats: This is the source's interpretation of Sorkin's framework, applied by extension to brand copy — it is not a tested ecommerce formula.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Treat Writing as Clear-Thinking Before Marketing
cards.summary: Writing forces clarity of thought; bad writing usually signals unclear ideas, not a style problem.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a product page, campaign, or proposal isn't landing with customers.
steps: Accept that 'I'm not a good writer' usually means the underlying idea isn't clear yet.
Use writing to surface fog: if you can't articulate the value proposition in plain language, clarify the value proposition before rewriting copy.
Prefer long-form drafting for important messages because bad thinking is harder to hide in a memo than in a slide deck.
Adopt the practice of writing narratives instead of slide-style decks for internal decisions (the source cites Amazon's PowerPoint ban and memo culture).
Treat writing as an idea generator too — expect new ideas to emerge during drafting, not just after.
caveats: The claim that 80% of writing is bad and cut to the good 20% is attributed to Paul Graham; treat it as a working heuristic, not a precise ratio.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx

cards.title: Write for the Internet: Unlearn School Rules
cards.summary: Reverse school-taught habits — word counts, fancy vocabulary, outlines — and favor concision and accessibility.
cards.use_when: Coaching writers or reviewing copy that feels bloated, padded, or overcomplicated for a store audience.
steps: Drop minimum word counts — padding is a school habit; concise usually wins on the internet.
Swap fancy vocabulary for accessible words; readers reward clarity, not vocabulary.
Replace formal outlines with a single subheadline or takeaway sentence that clarifies the piece's direction before drafting.
Recognize that 180-character subheadlines (as used under social post headlines) can serve as the working thesis.
Accept that headlines may be rewritten many times, but the subheadline often stays unchanged as the stabilizing anchor.
caveats: This is prescriptive advice calibrated to consumer internet writing; long-form technical or compliance content may still require structure and length.
cards.source_name: The 3-Step Writing Framework That Helped Us Build +$10M Newsletters.docx
